ABSTRACT This observational study investigated the potential influence of hormonal contraceptive (HC) use on selected hormonal biomarkers (estradiol, total testosterone, IGF‐1, cortisol, triiodothyronine, and leptin) that respond to diet and physical training–induced low energy availability (LEA). Thirty‐six female physique athletes—combined HC users ( n = 11), low‐dose progestin‐only HC users ( n = 11), and naturally menstruating females ( n = 14)—prepared for a physique competition. All participants voluntarily restricted energy intake while simultaneously participating in resistance training to maintain lean mass and aerobic training to increase energy expenditure. Measurements were completed over approximately 46 weeks as follows: before commencing the pre‐competition period, including dietary restriction and physical training (pre); after ∼23 weeks of dietary restriction and physical training (post); and after ∼23 weeks of recovery (recovery). Hormones were analyzed from fasting blood samples, whereas body mass, fat mass, fat‐free mass, and body fat percentage were measured using bioimpedance. Our main findings established that after ∼23 weeks of LEA, concentrations of estradiol and total testosterone remained stable in the combined HC users but decreased significantly in progestin‐only HC users and naturally menstruating females. Serum IGF‐1, triiodothyronine, and leptin decreased comparably from pre to post in all groups, whereas serum cortisol concentrations remained statistically unchanged throughout the investigation. These results indicate that the exogenous hormones in combined HCs users may maintain already suppressed hypothalamic–pituitary–ovarian axis function in the presence of LEA, whereas LEA‐induced changes in IGF‐1, triiodothyronine, and leptin may be comparable in combined and progestin‐only HC users and naturally menstruating females. Trial Registration The second study was registered at ClinicalTrials.gov ID: NCT04392752 Highlights Combined hormonal contraceptive users maintain already suppressed hypothalamic–pituitary–ovarian axis function in the presence of low energy availability (maintained estradiol and total testosterone concentrations), but hormonal contraceptive users and naturally menstruating females experience comparable, potentially negative, and endocrine consequences of low energy availability including significant decreases in concentrations of IGF‐1, triiodothyronine, and leptin. Hormonal contraceptive users and physicians prescribing hormonal contraceptives should be made aware that diet and physical training–induced low energy availability might negatively affect endocrine health. Roughly 50% of elite female athletes use HCs, where combined oral HCs are currently the most common (up to 70% of HC users) (Martin et al. 2018 ) and the use of hormonal (progestin‐only) intrauterine devices (IUDs) is increasing (Ekenros et al. 2022 ) although its prevalence is country‐dependent (Lindh et al. 2017 ; United Nations 2019 ). Combined HCs are composed of an estrogen (synthetic ethinyl estradiol) and a progestin (synthetic progesterone), where progestin‐only HCs contain only progestin. Combined HCs suppress hypothalamic–pituitary–ovarian (HPO) function, resulting in decreased pituitary gonadotropin secretion and lower concentrations of endogenous female sex steroids such as estradiol (E2) and progesterone (Rivera et al. 1999 ). Progestin‐only HCs may suppress HPO axis function in higher exogenous doses (Teal and Edelman 2021 ) whereas lower exogenous doses such as those delivered by minipills and hormonal IUDs do not suppress HPO axis function or do so inconsistently (Spencer et al. 2009 ; Grimes et al. 2013 ). As such, the endogenous sex steroid profile in low‐dose progestin‐only users may closely mimic that of naturally menstruating/eumenorrheic individuals (Spencer et al. 2009 ; Grimes et al. 2013 ). While the primary purpose of combined HCs is to suppress female sex steroid production, combined HCs also tend to decrease circulating concentrations of total and free testosterone with a concomitant increase in sex hormone binding globulin (SHBG) concentrations (Zimmerman et al. 2014 ). Combined HCs also tend to influence the hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal (HPA) axis resulting in higher total cortisol concentrations in combined HC users than nonusers (Hertel et al. 2017 ; Masama et al. 2022 ) although this observation is inconsistent (Kirschbaum et al. 1996 ; Larsen et al. 2020 ). An increase in growth hormone (GH) concentrations via estrogen's effect on the pituitary gland, concomitant with a decrease in insulin‐like growth factor 1 (IGF‐1), may be also observed in combined HC users (Southmayd and De Souza 2017 ; Birzniece and Ho 2021 ). The decrease in IGF‐1 may be due to estrogen's direct inhibitory effect on IGF‐1 synthesis in the liver or altered GH signaling; however, there does not appear to be significant differences in GH or IGF‐1 concentrations between naturally menstruating females and combined HC users (Massa et al. 1993 ; Riechman and Lee 2022 ; Özcan et al. 2024 ). Combined HCs, such as those containing, for example, dienogest and levonorgestrel, may increase thyroid hormones [total triiodothyronine (T3) and thyroxine (T4)] due to an increase in binding to serum globulins, but the free fractions of these hormones appear to be only slightly changed or unchanged (Torre et al. 2020 ). The systemic effects of progestin‐only HCs have not been as widely investigated, although it has been suggested that progestin‐only HCs only have a minor effect on systemic metabolism and inflammation (Wang et al. 2016 ). Indeed, progestin‐only pills containing desogestrel or levonorgestrel do not appear to significantly affect thyroid function (Kivelä et al. 2001 ). Low energy availability (LEA), an energy availability (EA) of < 30 kcal·kg −1 FFM·day −1 ], refers to a mismatch between dietary energy intakes (EI) to cover the energy cost of exercise (exercise energy expenditure, EEE), which results in suboptimal energy for physiological processes in the body, including those related to the maintenance of health and supporting training adaptations in athletes (Loucks et al. 2011 ). The equation EA = (EI−EEE)/FFM (where FFM = fat‐free mass) is often used to estimate EA, although protocols for evaluating EI, EEE, and FFM have not universally been agreed upon thus leaving some room for error (Burke et al. 2018 ). The effects of LEA, which may be induced by, for example, diet and physical training, on endocrine function have been reported in several publications (Elliott‐Sale et al. 2018 ; Ackerman and Misra 2018 ; Dipla et al. 2020 ; Areta et al. 2020 ; Ihalainen et al. 2024 ). For example, LEA has been reported to decrease gonadotropin‐releasing hormone resulting in downstream suppression of luteinizing hormone, estrogen, and testosterone whereas a decrease in thyroid hormones (e.g., T3), leptin, IGF‐1, and insulin and an increase in cortisol, growth hormone, and ghrelin have been reported (Elliott‐Sale et al. 2018 ; Ackerman and Misra 2018 ; Dipla et al. 2020 ; Areta et al. 2020 ; Ihalainen et al. 2024 ). Much of this research has focused on menstrual dysfunction and bone health, as well as the identification of surrogate markers of LEA in the context of the female athlete triad (Yeager et al. 1993 ; Otis et al. 1997 ) or relative energy deficiency in sport (REDs) (Mountjoy et al. 2014 , 2018 , 2023 ) models, whereas the possible influence of physical and psychological stressors on hormonal function are less discussed (Facchinetti et al. 1993 ; Nappi and Facchinetti 2003 ). To our knowledge, references to HC use in research on LEA in athletes (both in the triad and REDs models) are generally limited to reminders that (combined) HC provides exogenous hormones that suppress sex hormone concentrations that are likely to mask menstrual dysfunction, such as the ovulatory disorders (Munro et al. 2022 ), associated with LEA. At present, we are unaware of any literature that specifically discusses the possible influence of progestin‐only HC use on hormonal markers associated with LEA. Where exogenous sex steroids in combined HCs may continue to regulate the HPO axis when faced with LEA and other stressors, how other hormonal axes might respond to LEA and other stressors remains to be elucidated. Given the systemic hormonal changes induced by HCs as well as LEA (and other stressors), it is fair to hypothesize that the exogenous hormones in HCs may have implications for biomarkers used for monitoring athlete health. As such, the purpose of this observational study was to examine data (secondary analysis) from two physique athlete studies carried out at the University of Jyväskylä that was stratified into groups based on HC use (combined HC and progestin‐only HC) and nonuse that is, naturally menstruating females, in order to investigate the possible differences in responses between these groups in terms of changes in selected hormones after planned intentional exposure to LEA induced by diet and physical training. We hypothesized that combined HCs would maintain (already suppressed) concentrations of hormones associated directly with the HPO axis (estradiol and testosterone) during LEA but that combined HC and progestin‐only HC users would experience comparable endocrine changes to participants with natural cycles in hormones not directly regulated by the HPO axis, specifically IGF‐1, cortisol, triiodothyronine, and leptin.

molecular_mechanism_and_relationship.activity_type_context: The impact of combined hormonal contraceptive (HC) use, progestin-only HC use, and natural menstruation on physiological parameters in female physique athletes exposed to diet and physical training–induced Low Energy Availability (LEA).
molecular_mechanism_and_relationship.mechanism_description: Exogenous hormones in combined HCs may maintain already suppressed hypothalamic–pituitary–ovarian (HPO) axis function during LEA, preventing the LEA-induced decrease in estradiol and total testosterone observed in progestin-only HC users and naturally menstruating females. This maintenance may be due to testosterone conversion to estradiol, progesterone acting as a precursor for testosterone biosynthesis, or increased sex hormone binding globulin (SHBG) concentrations. LEA, induced by diet and physical training, generally leads to a decrease in gonadotropin-releasing hormone, suppressing luteinizing hormone, estrogen, and testosterone. LEA also appears to induce growth hormone (GH) resistance, impairing IGF-1 release from the liver and resulting in increased GH and decreased IGF-1. Decreased leptin concentrations, triggered by LEA, act via the hypothalamus to potentially increase appetite, decrease energy expenditure, suppress the HPO and HPT (hypothalamic-pituitary-thyroid) axes, and activate the HPA (hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal) axis. Combined HCs also suppress HPO function (decreasing pituitary gonadotropin and endogenous sex steroids), tend to decrease total/free testosterone while increasing SHBG, and can influence the HPA axis (higher total cortisol) and increase GH (via estrogen's effect), concomitantly decreasing IGF-1 (via direct liver inhibition or altered GH signaling). Combined HCs may also increase total triiodothyronine (T3) and thyroxine (T4) due to increased binding to serum globulins, with only slight or no changes in free fractions.

dose_intensity_and_specificity.dose_comparison_summary: The study compares the effects of distinct hormonal contexts (combined HC, progestin-only HC, natural menstruation) rather than varying doses of a single compound, in the presence of diet and physical training-induced Low Energy Availability (LEA). Higher exogenous doses of progestin-only HCs may suppress HPO axis function, whereas lower doses (e.g., minipills, hormonal IUDs) do not or do so inconsistently. After approximately 23 weeks of LEA, estradiol and total testosterone remained stable in combined HC users but decreased significantly in progestin-only HC users and naturally menstruating females. Serum IGF-1, triiodothyronine (T3), and leptin decreased comparably across all groups. Cortisol concentrations remained statistically unchanged in all groups, but were generally higher in combined HC users. LEA, defined as < 30 kcal·kg⁻¹ FFM·day⁻¹, is associated with increased GH and decreased IGF-1, and sustained lower T3. Short-term LEA (4 days) between 19.0 and 25.0 kcal·kg⁻¹ LBM·day⁻¹ can lead to a decrease in T3. During recovery, combined HC users had higher Energy Availability (EA) (> 40 kcal·kg⁻¹ FFM·day⁻¹) compared to other groups (< 30 kcal·kg⁻¹ FFM·day⁻¹), which corresponded with a significant increase in IGF-1, though not to the level of progestin-only HC users and naturally menstruating females. LEA appears to be a stronger stimulus for decreasing leptin than exercise stress alone.
dose_intensity_and_specificity.specificity_finding: Combined HC users specifically maintained stable estradiol and total testosterone concentrations during LEA, unlike progestin-only HC users and naturally menstruating females, due to the buffering effect of exogenous hormones against LEA-induced HPO axis declines. Conversely, LEA-induced decreases in IGF-1, triiodothyronine, and leptin were comparable across all groups, indicating a general effect of LEA independent of HC type. Serum cortisol concentrations remained statistically unchanged across time in all groups, but were significantly higher overall in combined HC users, demonstrating specific effects based on hormonal regimen. The free fraction of T3 appears minimally affected by combined HC use, suggesting its potential to respond to LEA regardless of HC type.

clinical_implication_and_population.target_population: Female physique athletes (n=36), including combined hormonal contraceptive users (n=11), low-dose progestin-only hormonal contraceptive users (n=11), and naturally menstruating females (n=14), preparing for competition through dietary restriction and physical training leading to low energy availability (LEA). This applies generally to physically active and athletic female populations of reproductive age.
clinical_implication_and_population.health_implication: Low energy availability (LEA), induced by diet and physical training, can negatively affect endocrine health in all female physique athletes, leading to potentially negative endocrine consequences such as significant decreases in IGF-1, triiodothyronine, and leptin, regardless of hormonal contraceptive use. Combined hormonal contraceptives (HCs) may mask LEA-induced hypothalamic–pituitary–ovarian axis dysfunction (e.g., by maintaining estradiol and total testosterone concentrations), potentially obscuring the physiological impact of LEA on endocrine health and ovulatory disorders. Decreased estradiol is associated with endocrine and menstrual dysfunction, decreased performance, bone health issues, reduced muscle mass and strength, and impaired metabolism and cardiovascular function. IGF-1 is crucial for promoting tissue growth, development, maintenance, muscle protein synthesis, and hypertrophy, which is important for physique and other athletes. Hormonal contraceptive users and prescribing physicians should be aware of LEA's negative effects on endocrine health.
clinical_implication_and_population.risk_classification: Adverse risk: Negative endocrine consequences of LEA, including significant decreases in IGF-1, triiodothyronine, and leptin. Decreased E2 resulting from LEA can lead to endocrine/menstrual dysfunction, bone health issues, and impaired performance. Diagnostic utility: Combined HCs can mask LEA-induced changes in HPO axis biomarkers (estradiol, total testosterone), making them unreliable indicators of LEA in these users. IGF-1 is a potential biomarker for identifying at least short-term LEA. Low bone mineral density, increased bone-related injuries, and decreased metabolic hormone concentrations (e.g., T3, sex hormones) can serve as signs for chronic problematic LEA in HC users. Protective benefit: Combined HCs may maintain E2 and tT concentrations in the presence of LEA, potentially mitigating some adverse effects related to their decline.

biomarker_reliability_and_future_focus.reliability_assessment: The study observed group-level patterns for estradiol, total testosterone, IGF-1, cortisol, triiodothyronine, and leptin in a relatively homogeneous sample of physique athletes. While data was extracted from studies not specifically designed for this research question, and menstrual cycle or HC use phases were not controlled, the observed patterns are suggested to be valid as they are not entirely cycle phase-dependent. Hormone analysis utilized chemical luminescence techniques (Immulite 2000; Siemens Healthineers), with estradiol measurement having 1.4% cross-reactivity for ethinyl estradiol. Limitations include the limited number of hormones investigated and small sample sizes. Research regarding the endocrine effects of LEA and other stressors on hormone concentrations in HC users is scarce; this study is acknowledged as one of the first to examine the possible influence of hormonal contraceptives on biomarkers commonly investigated in LEA, and further research is needed to confirm these findings. IGF-1 is considered a potential biomarker for identifying at least short-term LEA. The lack of significant change in cortisol concentrations over time may reflect maintained HPA axis homeostasis despite LEA. T3 shows potential to respond to LEA regardless of combined HC use.
recommended_alternatives: Decreased metabolic hormone concentrations (e.g., T3, sex hormones)
Further research in other athlete populations
Future investigations of the endocrine system in the female athlete triad and REDs paradigms should explicitly consider HC use
Additional research is required to explore cutoff values for hormonal indicators of LEA/REDs based on HC type
